καταλιμπάνει. τὸ παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὐχ ὁ
κόσμος παρέρχεται, ἀλλὰ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ παρόντος βίου μετα253 βάλλεται, ἡ φθορὰ
εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν, αἱ πόλεις, τὰ τείχη, οἱ νόμοι, αἱ γεωργίαι, αἱ τέχναι· ταῦτα γὰρ ὥσπερ
μορφή τις ἐπίκειται τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ ἥτις λαμβάνει μεταβολήν. 252,ξολ2 ∆ιὰ τούτου τὸ
ὀλιγοχρόνιον τῶν ἀνθρώπων δηλοῖ, ἵνα εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρήσωσιν ὡς φθάσαντες
τοῦ βίου τὸ τέλος τῶν προσκαίρων καταφρονήσαντες. εἰ δὲ καλόν ἐστι τοῖς ἔχουσιν
οὕτως ἔχειν ὡς μὴ ἔχουσιν, πῶς οὐ βέλτιον ἡ παρθενία; Τοῦτ' ἔστι μήτε τὰ λυπηρὰ
τοῦ βίου τούτου ὑμᾶς καταβαλλέτω, μήτε τὰ δοκοῦντα χαρᾶς ἄξια ὑπερευφραινέτω·
πάντα γὰρ τὰ ἐνταῦθα πρόσκαιρα καὶ οὐχ ἑστηκότα. Σχῆμα καὶ μορφή τις ὥσπερ τοῦ
κόσμου πολιτεῖαι, νόμοι, γεωρ253,ξολ2 γίαι, τέχναι, ἐμπορεῖαι, ὧν περισσὴ ἡ χρεία
τῆς φθορᾶς μεταβληθείσης εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν· δείκνυσιν οὖν ὅτι οὐχ ὁ κόσμος
παρέρχεται, ἀλλὰ τὸ παρὸν σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου. 1 Kor 7,32Ἔδειξε διὰ τί εἶπε τὸ ἐγὼ δὲ
ὑμῶν φείδομαι· ἵνα μὴ ἐν τοῖς μὴ μένουσι κενώσητε τὰς φροντίδας. καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς
τοῦτο μᾶλλον δείκνυσιν.Ἀπέδωκε τὴν αἰτίαν δι' ἣν τοῦ γάμου προτιμοτέρα ἡ
παρθενία· οὐ παρὰ τὴν κοίτην ἢ τὴν ἀποχὴν τῆς κοίτης, ἀλλὰ παρὰ τὸ τὸν γάμον
γέμειν φροντίδων τὸ κατὰ θεὸν ἀσχολεῖν εἰς τὴν εὐσέβειαν τὸν νοῦν. Θέλω ὑμᾶς
ἀμερίμνους εἶναι, ἵνα μὴ ἐν τοῖς μὴ μένουσι κενώσητε τὰς φροντίδας ταῖς βιωτικαῖς
περισπώμενοι χρείαις. διὸ καὶ τοῦ γάμου προτιμοτέρα ἡ παρθενία, οὐ διὰ τὴν ἀποχὴν
τῆς κοίτης, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἀπασχολεῖ τῆς εὐσεβείας τὸν νοῦν. 1 Kor 7,36–38 Νομίζουσί
τινες ὅτι αὐτόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτοῦ ἀσχημονεῖν λέγει, ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ παρθενίᾳ
εἴ τις ἀσχημονεῖν νομίζοι. οὐκ ἔστι δὲ οὕτως. καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς δείκνυσιν· λέγει γάρ· ὥστε
καὶ ὁ ἐκγαμίζων καλῶς ποιεῖ, ὁ δὲ μὴ ἐκγαμίζων κρεῖσσον ποιεῖ. οὐδεὶς δὲ ἑαυτὸν
ἐκγαμίζει, ἀλλ' ὑφ' ἑτέρου δίδοται. 1 Kor 7,40 Τὸ τοῦ μακαρίου τούτου κρεῖττον τὸ
οὕτω μεῖναι· τὸ μὲν γὰρ σωματικῆς ἐστιν ἀναπαύσεως, τὸ δὲ τελειοτέρας εὐσεβείας.
Πρὸς σύγκρισιν εἴρηται τοῦτο· μακαρία μὲν γάρ ἐστιν, ἐὰν γαμῆται καὶ ἔχῃ
προστασίαν ἀνδρός, μακαριωτέρα δέ, ἐὰν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν ἀποβλέπουσα μὴ γαμῆται,
ἀλλ' ἀπασχολήσῃ ἑαυτὴν τῷ θεῷ. 1 Kor 8,1–3Ἐπειδὴ οἱ Korίνθιοι τὰ εἰδωλόθυτα
ἤσθιον, λέγοντες ὅτι ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔστιν εἰδωλόθυτον–ἁγιάζω 254 γὰρ αὐτὰ τῇ
ἐπονομασίᾳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐσθίω–, δείκνυσιν αὐτὸς ὅτι οὐκ αὐτοὶ μόνοι ὡς σοφοὶ
ἴσασι τοῦτο, καὶ λέγει· οἴδαμεν ὅτι πάντες γνῶσιν ἔχομεν. ὥστε ὃ οἴδατε οἶδα, ὃ δὲ
πάσχετε οὐ πάσχω. Τοῦτο μέν, ὃ οἴδατε καὶ οἶδα, οὐ δεῖ σκοπεῖν· ὃ δὲ οἶδα, ὅτι δεῖ διὰ
τὸν ἀσθενῆ μὴ ἐσθίειν, τοῦτο οὐκ οἴδατε ὑμεῖς, ἐγὼ δὲ οἶδα. τί οὖν φυσιοῦσθε ὑπὸ
τῆς γνώσεως τῆς οὐ τοσοῦτον ἐχούσης ὅσον ἡ ἐμὴ γνῶσις; ἐπάγει γοῦν· εἰ δέ τις
δοκεῖ εἰδέναι τι ἐν ὑμῖν, οὐδέπω ἔγνωκεν καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι. αὐτίκα ὃ ἐγὼ οἶδα, σὺ
οὐδέπω οἶδας. εἰ δέ τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν θεόν, οὗτος ἔγνωσται ὑπ' αὐτοῦ. ἡμεῖς μὲν ὅπερ
ὡς ἄνθρωποι οἰηθῶμεν εἰδέναι, οὐδέπω οὐδὲν οἴδαμεν. τί δέ ἐστι τὸ μακάριον; τὸ
ἀγαπᾶν τὸν θεὸν καὶ γινώσκεσθαι ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, οὐκ ἐπειδὴ ἀγνοεῖ τοὺς μὴ ἀγαπῶντας,
ἀλλ' ὅτι οἰκειοῦται τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας· λαμβάνεται γὰρ τὸ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ ἐπὶ
οἰκειώσεως, ὥσπερ τὸ τῆς ἀγνοίας καὶ ἐπὶ ἀλλοτριώσεως, οἷόν ἐστι τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ
κυρίου ῥηθὲν τὸ ἀπέλθετε, οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς. 253,ξολ2Ἐπειδὴ οἱ Korίνθιοι
ἔλεγον· οὐδὲν εἴδωλόν ἐστιν, διὸ καὶ οὐ λογοῦμεν τὰ ἱερόθυτα μᾶλλον ἐν 254,ξολ2
τῇ ὀνομασίᾳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐσθίοντες ἢ βλαπτόμεθα, δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὐκ αὐτοὶ μόνοι ὡς
σοφοὶ ἴσασι τοῦτο ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλοι, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι τι ἱερόθυτον· ὥστε ὃ μὲν οἴδατε οἶδα,
ὃ δὲ πάσχετε οὐ πάσχω. ἡ μὲν οὖν τοιαύτη γνῶσις φυσιοῖ καὶ βλάπτει, ἐὰν τὸ ἑαυτῶν
οἴδητε, οὐ μὴν καὶ τὸ ἄλλο ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ, καὶ δεῖ γάρ σε διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ
pass_a_gloss: [7:29-31, first form, continued from the previous section] ...he leaves [the need] in place. For 'the form of this world passes away' shows that the world does not pass away, but the form of the present life changes, corruption into incorruption: the cities, the walls, the laws, the farming, the crafts. For these lie on this life like a kind of shape, which receives change. [Second form, page 252 column 2] By this he shows the short time of human beings, so that they may go on to repentance as having reached the end of life, having come to despise temporary things. [Second form, not printed again because the first form has it in the previous section: and if it is good for those who have to have as not having, how is virginity not better?] That is, let neither the painful things of this life throw you down, nor let the things that seem worthy of joy make you rejoice too much; for all things here are temporary and not standing. A form and a kind of shape of the world, as it were, are civic life, laws, farming, crafts, trading, of which the need is superfluous when corruption has been changed into incorruption. [Not printed again: so he shows that not the world passes away but the present form of the world.] [Label 1 Kor 7,32] He showed why he said 'but I spare you': so that you may not empty out your cares on things that do not remain. And what follows shows this more. He gave the reason for which virginity is more preferred than marriage: not because of the bed or the abstention from the bed, but because of marriage being full of cares, [and] the occupying of the mind, according to God, with piety. [Second form, not printed again: I want you to be without care, so that you may not empty your cares on things that do not remain, being distracted by the needs of life; therefore virginity is preferred to marriage, not because of the abstention from the bed, but because it (marriage) draws the mind away from piety.] [Label 1 Kor 7,36-38] Some think that he says a man behaves unseemly about himself, as if instead 'if anyone thinks he behaves unseemly toward his own virginity'. But it is not so. And what follows shows it; for he says: 'so that both the one giving in marriage does well, and the one not giving in marriage does better.' But no one gives himself in marriage, but is given by another. [Label 1 Kor 7,40] This blessed man's 'better' is to remain so; for the one is of bodily rest, the other of more perfect piety. This is said for comparison: for she is blessed if she is married and has the protection of a husband, but more blessed if, looking toward piety, she is not married but occupies herself fully with God. [Label 1 Kor 8,1-3] Since the Corinthians were eating idol-sacrifices, saying that for us there is no idol-sacrifice (for I sanctify them by naming Christ over them, and I eat), he himself shows that not they alone as wise men know this, and he says: 'we know that we all have knowledge.' So what you know I know, but what you suffer I do not suffer. This, what you know and I know, need not be examined; but what I know, that one must not eat because of the weak one, this you do not know, but I know. Why then are you puffed up by the knowledge that does not have as much as my knowledge has? He adds then: 'if anyone among you thinks he knows something, he has not yet known as one must know.' For instance, what I know, you do not yet know. 'But if anyone loves God, this one has been known by him.' We, what we as human beings might suppose we know, do not yet know anything. And what is the blessed thing? To love God and to be known by him, not since he does not know those not loving, but because he makes his own those who love; for the word of knowing is taken also for making one's own, as that of not knowing also for estranging, such as the word spoken by the Lord: 'depart, I never knew you.' [Second form, page 253 column 2; not printed again: since the Corinthians said: an idol is nothing, so we bless (Greek λογοῦμεν) the temple-sacrifices, eating them in the naming of Christ, rather than being harmed, he shows that not they alone as wise know this but others too, that there is no temple-sacrifice; so what you know I know, but what you suffer I do not suffer.] Such knowledge, then, puffs up and harms, if you know your own [point], but not also the other one, that love builds up; and indeed you must, because of the love of the... [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: …he leaves in place. The words “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31) show that the world itself does not pass away. What changes is the form of the present life, corruption turning into incorruption: cities, walls, laws, farming, crafts. These lie over this life like a kind of outward shape, and it is that shape which undergoes change.

The second catena form adds: By this he makes plain how brief human life is, so that people may turn to repentance, as men who have already reached the end of life and so look down on passing things. That is: do not let the griefs of this life cast you down, and do not let what seems worth rejoicing over carry you away with joy, for everything here is passing and does not stand. The form and shape of the world, as it were, are its civic life, laws, farming, crafts and trade, and none of them will be needed once corruption has been changed into incorruption.

On 1 Corinthians 7:32: He has shown why he said, “But I am sparing you” (1 Corinthians 7:28): so that you do not pour out your cares on things that do not last. What follows shows this still more clearly. He has given the reason why virginity is preferred to marriage. It is not the marriage bed, or abstaining from it, but that marriage is full of cares, and that the mind should be occupied, as God wills, with devotion.

On 1 Corinthians 7:36–38: Some think he means a man behaving shamefully toward himself, as if the sense were, “if anyone thinks he is behaving shamefully toward his own virginity.” That is not so, and what follows proves it, for he says, “So then he who gives her in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better” (1 Corinthians 7:38). Nobody gives himself in marriage; one is given by someone else.

On 1 Corinthians 7:40: In the judgment of this blessed man, the better course is to remain as she is. Marriage belongs to bodily ease; remaining belongs to a more perfect devotion. This is said by way of comparison. She is blessed if she marries and has a husband to protect her, but more blessed if, with her eyes on devotion, she does not marry and gives herself wholly to God.

On 1 Corinthians 8:1–3: The Corinthians were eating food offered to idols and saying, “For us there is no such thing as idol food; I make it holy by calling on the name of Christ, and I eat.” So he shows that they are not the only wise ones who know this, and says, “We know that we all have knowledge.” In other words: what you know, I know too, but what you suffer, I do not suffer. What you know and I know is not the point to look at. What I know, that one must not eat for the sake of the weak, you do not know, but I do. Why then are you puffed up by a knowledge that comes nowhere near mine? So he goes on: “If anyone among you thinks he knows something, he has not yet known as he ought to know.” For example, what I know, you do not yet know. “But if anyone loves God, he is known by him.” Whatever we, as human beings, may suppose we know, we do not yet know anything. And what is blessedness? To love God and to be known by him. This is not because he is unaware of those who do not love him, but because he makes those who love him his own. “Knowing” is used for making someone one's own, just as “not knowing” is used for estrangement, as in the Lord's words, “Depart; I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23).

The second catena form adds: Knowledge of this kind, then, puffs up and does harm if you know only your own point and not the other one as well, that love builds up. For out of love you must also, for the sake of the…

choices.why: The sentence begins in u03-rem-close (τὴν μέντοι χρείαν καταλιμπάνει: he removes excess enjoyment but leaves need in place); the section opens mid-sentence, so an ellipsis.
rejected: It leaves behind (old English, no subject or object)

choices.why: ἐκγαμίζω is to give in marriage; Severianus's argument (no one gives himself in marriage) depends on it.

choices.english: In the judgment of this blessed man, the better course
choices.why: τοῦ μακαρίου τούτου is Paul; the article takes κρεῖττον as his verdict.
rejected: It is better for this blessed one (old English)

choices.term: τὸ κατὰ θεὸν ἀσχολεῖν εἰς τὴν εὐσέβειαν τὸν νοῦν
choices.english: and that the mind should be occupied, as God wills, with devotion
choices.why: Second bare articular infinitive after παρὰ τό; rendered as a second reason without supplying a subject.
rejected: the mind, which is filled with the cares of marriage, is occupied in godliness (old English, makes marriage the subject)

choices.english: what you suffer, I do not suffer
choices.why: Kept literal; Severianus contrasts shared knowledge with the Corinthians' condition (being puffed up).

choices.english: first form printed; second form only where it adds
choices.why: Brief rule on doublets; the second form is marked by 252,col2 and 253,col2 in the edition.
